articles.title: World Series 2026: For Milwaukee Brewers, finally winning a title is a celebration decades in the making
articles.summary: The 2026 Brewers were a complete collective, built meticulously from the inside out, from the bottom up.
articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — They came from Wisconsin.

From Waukesha and Menomonie and Lake Nebagamon and, of course, Milwaukee. They flew and drove through the night and skipped class and played hooky to witness history and make forever memories and drink the Gulf Coast dry. Into this dome, they crammed an entire state and 56 years of dreaming and generations of heartbreak. So when the Milwaukee Brewers finally did the darn thing , capturing the franchise's first World Series title, Florida sounded like Wisconsin.

As the Brewers players charged from the dugout, leaping and jumping and cussing in disbelief, the traveling faithful thundered in joyous unison. Tears, everywhere. Soon, fans began cramming themselves four or five deep atop the third-base dugout, just to get as close to the action as possible. When the trophy ceremony finally commenced, Tropicana Field was still nearly 60% full, mostly with Brewers fans. It was a remarkable sight.

"Really, it was a home game," president of baseball operations Matt Arnold told Yahoo Sports in the champagne-soaked aftermath of his team's 4-1, title-clinching victory on Wednesday in Game 5 . "I'm so happy for the people of Wisconsin. It's a big deal."

Arnold, the engineer of this masterpiece, lumbered up the dugout steps and onto the diamond to join the chaotic victory celebration. Almost immediately, he crossed paths with an exultant Christian Yelich, a broad grin pasted on his boyish face. The two men embraced, bear-hugging each other, the architect and the captain.

"You did it!" Yelich bellowed, pointing a finger into Arnold's chest.

"No, we did it! We did it!" Arnold shot back.

Arnold, as he often is these days, was correct. This Brewers club was a complete collective , even more than any other champion in recent memory. It was a group built meticulously, from the inside out, from the bottom up. Backup catcher Gary Sánchez was the only player on Milwaukee's World Series roster acquired via free agency. Seven of the 10 Brewers in the Game 5 starting lineup were originally drafted or signed by the club.

Together, an enormous army of front-office quants, scouts, analysts and evaluators with cockamamie titles and nebulous responsibilities built a juggernaut centered on homegrown cornerstones. They overcame the barriers and inconveniences of life in a small market to build what is widely considered the best organization in the sport.

And while this unit wasn't devoid of stars — Jacob Misiorowski will win the NL Cy Young Award, World Series MVP William Contreras is a generational catcher , Jackson Chourio established himself as a superstar on the rise — they operated as a single organism, exhibiting dominance in the sum of the parts. In particular, the offense's commitment to a patient, high-contact, opposite-field identity was as selfless as it was abnormal in today's swing-for-the fences game.

"I'm most proud of where the lineup came together, man," NLCS MVP Jake Bauers told Yahoo Sports after the game. "The way the lineup came together and bought in to a singular approach. One through nine, and all we did, the rest of the season, was f***ing executed."

Bauers became an unexpected breakout star of this postseason, gaining recognition for his calm demeanor during lengthy, almost gladiatorial plate appearances. A free agent this offseason , the blond-bearded first baseman refashioned himself from an afterthought castaway into a middle-of-the-order force. When he handed manager Pat Murphy the game ball from the final out, Murphy responded with a hilariously incisive quip that only the quick-tongued skipper could've conjured.

"You're going to be a rich f***er, Jake," he declared. "Just remember, when you're on that horses*** Yankees team and you guys are all playing for yourself, just remember — this is the way we used to do it."

Comical conjecture aside, there's an element of truth in Murphy's assessment. This Brewers club will be remembered through halcyon eyes, with layers of nostalgia.

That is, in large part, because this team was undeniably good.

Nobody will look back on the 2026 Brewers and wonder why they won it all. They finished the regular season with the most wins, beat a lava-hot Padres team in the NLDS, swept the two-time defending champion Dodgers in the NLCS and then clobbered the American League's best club in a five-game Fall Classic beatdown .

Their performance in a comparatively boring and straightforward Game 5 clincher perfectly exemplified that dynamic. Misiorowski wasn't quite at his world-beating best , notching just two strikeouts, his fewest in a start all year, yet the mound gave him more trouble than the Rays' lineup. Stellar showings from the defense and bullpen kept Tampa Bay off the board until the ninth. And while the top of Milwaukee's offense struggled to get things started, the bottom offered the spark against Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen, starting on three days' rest.

Rookie Cooper Pratt, the would-be Game 4 hero , laced an RBI single to open the scoring in the second. And when Rasmussen exited after four, the Brewers' relentless lineup went to work. Three straight singles from the 7, 8 and 9-hole hitters doubled the score in the fifth. One inning later, World Series MVP William Contreras banged a double off the left-field wall to drive in Yelich and then came around to score himself. Tampa plated one in the ninth off closer Trevor Megill, but the Rays never seriously threatened to take the lead.

It was a commanding, emphatic, undeniable showing, one that produced waterworks from Whitewater to Wauwatosa. Misiorowski cried during his postgame interview on the broadcast. Yelich choked up talking about the late Brewers icon Bob Uecker. Arnold, too, admitted to holding back tears.

"The things that have flashed ... the miles, the minutes, the late nights, the early mornings, the flights, the meetings, the handbooks that we've written — all that nerdy stuff," he told Yahoo Sports.

In that way, Wednesday evening was, above all else, a culmination. A deserved celebration decades in the making.

Crack a cold one, Wisconsin. You've certainly earned it.

articles.title: Everything to Know on Expected MLB Lockout, Free Agency and More Key Offseason Dates
articles.summary: The 2026 MLB season officially came to a close on Wednesday night when the Milwaukee Brewers finished off the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 5 to claim the first World Series title in franchise history.
articles.body:
The 2026 MLB season officially came to a close on Wednesday night when the Milwaukee Brewers finished off the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 5 to claim the first World Series title in franchise history.

Now the offseason begins, and it's going to be a weird one.

The current collective bargaining agreement is set to expire this winter, and a lockout is widely expected as the owners and the MLBPA try to come to terms on a variety of issues, including the potential implementation of a salary cap.

1 Player Every Team Should Re-Sign in 2026-27 MLB Free Agency

Way-Too-Early Predictions for 2027 MLB Playoffs 🔮

There are plenty of offseason boxes to be checked before a lockout could take effect, and the to-do list kicks into gear almost immediately now that the Commissioner's Trophy has been handed out.

Let's take a stroll through MLB's winter timeline with all the key dates leading up to the expiration of the current CBA, and the timetable that the two sides will have to get a new CBA on the books without sacrificing any of the 2027 MLB season.

Nov. 2: Deadline to Extend Qualifying Offers, Exercise Contract Options

The first step of each MLB offseason is a five-day window for teams and players to sort out contract options, as club, player and mutual options all need to be exercised or declined within that short window.

That's also the window of time when a player can exercise an opt-out clause in his current contract, and Mets third baseman Bo Bichette's opt-out decision will be one of the more compelling early storylines.

Teams also have that same five-day window to extend qualifying offers to eligible free agents. In order to be eligible, a player must have spent the entire season with his club and not have received a qualifying offer in the past.

This year's qualifying offer will be a one-year, $23.15 million contract, with Ryan Jeffers (MIN), Brandon Lowe (PIT), David Bednar (NYY) and Adrian Morejón (SD) among the bubble candidates who could consider accepting. If a player receives a qualifying offer and rejects it, his former team will receive draft pick compensation when he signs elsewhere.

Nov. 12: Deadline to Accept/Reject Qualifying Offer

Once qualifying offers have been handed out, players have 10 days to decide whether to accept or reject the one-year, $23.15 million deal.

The Rookie of the Year (Nov. 9), Manager of the Year (Nov. 10), Cy Young (Nov. 11) and MVP (Nov. 12) awards are all voted on by the Baseball Writers Association of America, and the winners are announced across a four-day stretch.

Pete Crow-Armstrong and Yordan Alvarez are heavy favorites for MVP honors, Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler sit atop their respective Cy Young races and Kevin McGonigle is expected to be the unanimous AL Rookie of the Year winner. That leaves little drama in this year's award races.

The most compelling debate is NL Rookie of the Year, where Reds slugger Sal Stewart is the favorite over Mets teammates Carson Benge and Nolan McLean, while Cardinals second baseman JJ Wetherholt is also a candidate.

The annual winter meetings are one of the highlights of the MLB offseason, as they often bring a flurry of activity in free agency and on the trade market.

The GM meetings and owners meetings generally receive considerably less fanfare, filling a more behind-the-scenes role in laying the groundwork for the offseason ahead.

This year could generate a few more headlines, particularly at the owners meetings, as it will be an opportunity for them to come together to discuss their side of the CBA negotiations.

Expect at least a few useful nuggets to trickle out to the press on what the owners will be looking for when they sit down at the CBA negotiating table.

It's also worth wondering if there might be more transaction activity than normal at the GM meetings, as teams look to make moves ahead of a potential lockout.

The non-tender deadline marks the annual decision each MLB team faces on whether to offer or "tender" a contract to the arbitration-eligible players on their roster.

If they tender a contract, the team and player can continue to negotiate a salary figure for the upcoming season in an effort to avoid an arbitration hearing. If they do not tender a contract, the player is considered to be "non-tendered" and immediately becomes a free agent.

Outfielder Adolis García was the biggest name cut loose at the non-tender deadline a year ago, while JJ Bleday, Nathaniel Lowe and Jonah Heim are among the other non-tendered players who ended up providing solid value with their next team.

Former top prospects Nolan Gorman (STL) and Triston Casas (BOS), and past All-Star selections Josiah Gray (WAS), Zach McKinstry (DET) and Camilo Doval (SF) are among the notable non-tender candidates this year.

The current CBA expires on Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point the expectation is that the owners will lock out the players and the offseason will grind to a halt.

"On Dec. 1, after years of saber-rattling and months of performative proposals, the 30 owners will lock out the players and shut down the sport. The substantive negotiating for the next collective bargaining agreement may not take place until February or March," wrote Andy McCullough of The Athletic .

Whether that means an expedited market prior to the expected lockout, or an unofficial freeze on any transactions ahead of an unknown salary situation in the future remains to be seen.

Major League Baseball proposed a $245.3 million salary cap and $171.2 million salary floor in preliminary negotiations back in May, while the MLBPA has given no indication it will accept a salary cap in any form.

An overhaul to the arbitration system and a potential international draft are also talking points, but the salary cap discussion will be the biggest hurdle to avoiding missed games.

Plenty of words will be written on the moving parts of the next labor deal in the coming months, but Dec. 1 is the date to circle when the sport is widely expected to shut down.

The expectation is that the lockout will mean cancelling the annual winter meetings, with no business to be done while the league is shut down.

Feb. 19, 2027: Start of Spring Training Games

The first spring training games to ramp up for the 2027 season are scheduled for Feb. 19, and this is the first date that could indicate that the CBA negotiations are putting the 2027 season in jeopardy if there is still a lockout in place.

The last time the CBA expired, a lockout began on Dec. 2 and stretched all the way to March 10 for a total of 99 days that the league was shuttered.

Opening Day was originally scheduled for March 31 for the 2022 season, and the delayed start of spring training ultimately pushed that to April 7. No games were lost, as a full 162-game season was played.

All of that to say, it's possible that the lockout could stretch into the start of spring training without impacting Opening Day, but with far more substantial issues on the table, it's unclear just how long a lockout might stretch this time around.

articles.title: 1 Player Every Team Should Re-Sign in 2026-27 MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: MLB's financial landscape could look very different in November than it does when the next collective bargaining agreement is in place.
articles.body:
MLB's financial landscape could look very different in November than it does when the next collective bargaining agreement is in place.

While we don't know whether there will be a salary cap in the next CBA, we do know that it's going to be business as usual for the first few weeks of the offseason, until the owners lock the players out when the current agreement expires on Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET.

Let's take a look at one player every team should re-sign this offseason, even if we aren't necessarily sure how it will affect them moving forward.

Rays ace Drew Rasmussen called Nick Martinez "the best teammate ever" back in July when he earned his first career All-Star Game selection.

On top of earning love from his new clubhouse, Martinez was damn good on the mound in 2026. Across 180 innings, Martinez went 15-6 with a 3.10 ERA for the eventual AL Champions.

Martinez will be 36. We know the Rays have typically been more inclined to churn things than to retain more expensive veterans. Martinez is ineligible for the qualifying offer, which isn't ideal. The Rays would badly miss his presence—both on and off the mound—if they don't retain him.

You always run the risk of going to the well one too many times when signing relievers, especially to multi-year deals. Bednar was tremendous in his first full season in pinstripes, racking up 35 saves and posting a 2.47 ERA across 64 games.

Bednar will pitch next season at 32 years old, but he should have no issue getting at least three years in free agency. The Yankees would be wise to try to retain the anchor of their bullpen.

Given that he was unhappy with being pulled after 4.2 innings in Game 2 of the ALWCS, Gray might decline his $30 million club option for 2027. Even if he loved his season in Boston, opting out and returning to the open market this offseason might be the best business decision for Gray.

He may not make $30 million in 2027 if he opts out, but after going 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA in 169 innings this past year, Gray can get a larger overall guarantee. Gray is better than Merrill Kelly, who landed a two-year, $40 million deal last winter as he entered his age-37 season. Gray will be 37 in November.

If Gray opts out, the Red Sox will owe him a $5 million buyout. They may not be inclined to re-sign him on top of that, but even with Ranger Suárez, Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle and Brayan Bello already in the fold for next season, the Red Sox would really miss Gray if they let him go.

The Orioles elected not to trade Trevor Rogers prior to the trade deadline, which makes you think that president of baseball operations Mike Elias would like to retain the lefty.

For the O's, the best arrangement might be for Rogers to accept the one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer. That would give them more time to evaluate Rogers, who has shown flashes of greatness but has not been able to sustain them. For example, Rogers disappointed in the first half, posting a 4.48 ERA over 17 starts. He was much better after the All-Star Break, finishing with a 3.52 ERA in 13 second-half starts.

The more complicated scenario for Baltimore would be deciding what to do if Rogers—who turns 29 in November—declines the QO.

42-year-old Max Scherzer, 37-year-old George Springer, 37-year-old Patrick Corbin and Shane Bieber—who has made 20 total starts over the last three seasons—are among the free agents the Blue Jays have this offseason.

Considering they responded to a Game 7 World Series loss in 2025 by going 79-83 in 2026, there isn't really a free agent worth re-signing for general manager Ross Atkins.

Because the Guardians don't sign many free agents or keep players into their last year of arbitration eligibility, it's slim pickings here.

Austin Hedges has 93 defensive runs saved in his career, which is why he's played 12 years in the majors despite being a .190 hitter. If the Guardians are able to bring back Hedges to be the 1B catcher behind Patrick Bailey, that would make sense.

Sean Newcomb signed a one-year, $4.5 million deal with the White Sox last offseason.

That investment by general manager Chris Getz proved to be one of the better moves of the offseason, as Newcomb made 60 regular-season appearances and posted a 3.09 ERA. For good measure, he pitched to a 2.57 ERA over seven postseason frames.

It will take more than $4.5 million to bring Newcomb back, but he pitched well enough that the White Sox should want to retain him.

The Twins acquired A.J. Minter from the New York Mets before the trade deadline. The veteran lefty pitched to a 2.78 ERA in 25 games for Minnesota. Overall, he posted a 2.56 ERA in 48 games in 2026.

Tom Pohlad is trying to change his family's reputation as the control person of the Twins. Bringing back a 33-year-old lefty reliever won't do that, but it would be a small gesture showing the organization is putting its best foot forward to compete in 2027.

After playing in Japan and South Korea from 2022 to 2025, Anderson returned stateside in 2026 on a one-year, $7 million deal with the Tigers. Across 49 games and 11 starts, Anderson posted a 3.67 ERA.

The Tigers could pick up his $10 million club option for 2027, although th ere is no buyout if they decline it. Scott Harris and the Tigers could also decline the option and try to bring Anderson back at a lower price as a swingman.

With Carlos Estévez ($11.1 million), Jonathan India ($8 million) and Matt Strahm ($7.5 million) coming off the books, the Royals will have some money to work with as president of baseball operations J.J. Picollo looks to retool the team after consecutive disappointing seasons.

You could definitely argue that there aren't any impending free agents Kansas City should bring back. However, the $2.5 million club option on Tony Gonsolin is intriguing, even though he made just one appearance for the team before an allergic reaction ended his season.

Gonsolin hasn't been particularly durable, but he went 26-6 with a 2.51 ERA in 59 games for the Los Angeles Dodgers from 2019 to 2022. That upside is still intriguing.

After posting a 2.30 ERA in 275 games between 2022 and 2025, Bryan Abreu seemed headed for a monster contract this offseason. Unfortunately, that likely won't happen after he posted a 3.73 ERA in 66 games this past season.

However, Abreu was lights-out after the All-Star Game, pitching to a 1.71 ERA in 32 appearances. He's still only 29 years old and has a long track record of success in Houston. Whether it's a one-year, prove-it deal or a relatively lucrative multi-year deal, the Astros are the best spot for Abreu.

For as disastrous as Joc Pederson's first season with the Rangers was, the veteran slugger bounced back in the second and final season of a $37 million deal. He should really only play against right-handed pitching, but he's excellent against righties, as shown by his 25 homers and .834 OPS in 2026.

Pederson and the Rangers have a mutual $18.5 million option for a third season to decide on. Typically, mutual options get declined by at least one side. It would be wise for the Rangers to find a way to keep Pederson in the fold.

It kind of feels like the Mariners will give Randy Arozarena a qualifying offer and then be happy to collect the draft-pick compensation when he departs in free agency.

That may prove to be the best decision for the franchise. While Arozarena posted an .865 OPS in his contract year, he produced a .761 OPS between 2022 and 2024. There's risk in paying guys after their contract seasons.

That said, it's been historically difficult for the Mariners to attract impact offensive talent to T-Mobile Park, which isn't hitter-friendly. Arozarena was better on the road this past year, but still posted a .788 OPS in home games, so maybe president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto should think about trying to retain the former ALCS MVP.

The Athletics will likely pray that Luis Severino declines his $22 million player option for 2026 after he posted a 4.43 ERA in 41 starts over two seasons in Sacramento.

Other than Severino, things should be pretty easy this offseason. The A's will decline Jeff McNeil's $15.8 million club option and Jeffrey Springs' $15 million club option. Other veteran free agents like Mark Leiter Jr. and Jonah Heim will be easy decisions not to bring back.

Unless you're tempted to pick up Robert Stephenson's $2.5 million club option—which the Angels likely won't be after he made 12 appearances in three seasons in Anaheim—there's not much to pick from here.

The good news is that there is new ownership with Stan Kroenke. He'll now get to put his desired president of baseball operations and manager in place. There's really nowhere to go but up for a franchise that's coming off its 11th consecutive losing season.

Not only did Mauricio Dubón drive in 73 runs after being acquired from the Astros, but he also saw time at shortstop, second base, third base, left field and center field. He was particularly impressive at shortstop, where he posted one defensive run saved and five outs above average.

It will likely take a multi-year deal to bring back the 32-year-old, but the Braves would badly miss Dubón's versatility if they let him walk in free agency.

In parts of five seasons, Edmundo Sosa has established himself as one of the best utility players in Phillies history. He can mash left-handed pitching and plays shortstop, second base, third base and left field. Plus, he's a tremendous person.

It's unclear if the Phillies will re-sign the 30-year-old. There are a lot of moving parts in their infield, with uncertainty about Trea Turner's position and both Alec Bohm and Luis Arraez set to become free agents. That could mean it makes even more sense to retain Sosa, although top prospect Aidan Miller is looming and Bryce Harper is returning to first base, so there are only so many seats.

Still, if the Phillies don't bring Sosa back, they'll miss his flexibility and clubhouse presence.

The Marlins will certainly exercise Sandy Alcantara's $21 million club option after he led baseball with 214 innings pitched this past season. They could still trade the former NL Cy Young Award winner, who is set to become a free agent after 2027.

Their only other real free agent is Pete Fairbanks, who struggled with a 6.31 ERA in 46 games for the Fish in 2026. It's fair to say they won't be bringing Fairbanks back after giving the veteran reliever $13 million in free agency last offseason.

Miles Mikolas was released by the Nationals in August after posting a 5.82 ERA across 116 innings. He would have been their only free agent this offseason.

President of baseball operations Paul Toboni will still be plenty busy this offseason. Most notably, he'll have to decide whether the Nats listen to offers on CJ Abrams and James Wood, who are two and three years away from free agency, respectively.

The Mets overturned so much of their roster last winter that their only real free agent decision to make will be whether Bo Bichette opts out of the final two seasons of his three-year, $126 million contract.

Even in what is projected to be a weak free-agent market, Bichette might opt into his second year of this deal after posting a 97 OPS+ in his first season with the Mets.

If Bichette opts out, you can definitely make the case that the Mets should try to retain him. Then again, he doesn't really have a position and underwhelmed for a last-place team in 2026. Re-signing him if he opts out might turn out to be chasing your losses for president of baseball operations David Stearns.

Considering Andrew Vaughn has one remaining year of arbitration eligibility, the Brewers may feel comfortable letting Jake Bauers walk after a career year in which he won NLCS MVP.

But if you're just looking at the greatest season in franchise history and who it would make sense to try to keep, it's hard to imagine the Brewers not being worse without a guy who posted a 140 OPS+ in 2026. Of course, every year the Brewers lose an impact player; the show just seems to go on.

Still, it feels like this might be a guy the Brewers should try to retain on a two-year deal.

Seiya Suzuki just completed a five-year, $85 million deal. Based on how he performed in his contract season, Suzuki should get another five-campaign pact, this time with a larger total value.

Again, the Cubs could let him walk if he declines the qualifying offer. But like, this is the Chicago Cubs. Suzuki posted an .823 OPS in five seasons on the north side. Even if he could eventually wind up at DH, why would the Cubs not bring back Suzuki and keep him in the lineup with Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman?

At the very least, the Pirates should extend a one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer to Brandon Lowe, who homered 35 times and drove in 96 runs after being acquired from the Rays.

The Buccos could let Lowe walk in free agency and collect draft-pick compensation if he declines the qualifying offer, which he almost certainly will. But with likely limited time remaining with Paul Skenes in Pittsburgh, the smarter move would be to give Lowe a lucrative multi-year deal and build a playoff team around the former NL Cy Young Award winner.

Ryne Stanek is the only notable free agent for the Cardinals this offseason, which shouldn't be surprising, given that president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom turned over the roster last offseason.

Stanek did log 70 games for the RedBirds in 2026, but posted a 4.52 FIP during that stretch, so he's unlikely to return.

Even though he'll pitch next season at 36, Emilio Pagán should be someone the Reds try to re-sign. Pagán has a 3.07 ERA in 115 games over the past two seasons, despite pitching his home games at the bandbox of Great American Ball Park.

Eugenio Suárez's second go-round with the Reds didn't go as planned, so they'll surely decline their half of a $16 million mutual option for 2027.

The Dodgers will be the odds-on favorite to sign Tarik Skubal this offseason, but it shouldn't be viewed as fait accompli that the two-time AL Cy Young Award winner will stay in Los Angeles.

If Skubal—a Scott Boras client—is intent on signing before the lockout, will the Dodgers feel comfortable giving him a record-setting deal without knowing the future financial landscape? Is owner Mark Walter in a position to doll out a megadeal this offseason?

Obviously, if all things are equal, the Dodgers should re-sign Tarik Skubal. They'll be much worse without him. But this is a team that's let Manny Machado, Corey Seager, Max Scherzer and Trea Turner walk in free agency in the past, so it's not as though it would be unprecedented for Skubal to turn out to be just a short-term Dodger.

President of baseball operations A.J. Preller is always active. He's going to have his work cut out for him as he tries to rebuild basically the entire starting rotation in San Diego this offseason.

His first move should be to give Michael King—who has a 3.15 ERA in parts of three seasons since being acquired from the Yankees—a long-term deal. He'll likely opt out of the final two seasons of a three-year, $75 million deal . King will be ineligible for the qualifying offer after receiving it last offseason, so the Padres will be left empty-handed if the 31-year-old departs as a free agent.

Long-time ace Zac Gallen will surely depart after he posted a 6.07 ERA in 2026. But another veteran arm—righty Michael Soroka—is someone the Snakes should aim to re-sign. He posted a 3.41 ERA over 116 innings in 2026.

Merrill Kelly will be 38 in 2027. Eduardo Rodríguez had a great 2026, but you never know what you'll get from him year to year. He's also been injured relatively frequently in his career. It's unclear whether Brandon Pfaadt can replicate the success he had after returning from Triple-A.

This is not a team that's going to get through next season with only five starters, so bringing back a guy like Soroka would be wise.

Technically, there's not a great answer here. However, if the Giants can find a way for him to coexist with Marcelo Mayer and Casey Schmitt, it would be interesting for them to reunite with Luis Arraez. Before being traded to the Phillies, Arraez was hitting .324, including .361 at Oracle Park.

Kyle Freeland, Jose Quintana, Tomoyuki Sugano and Jordan Romano will all become free agents . Of that veteran pitching quartet, are any of them worth bringing back to the 104-loss Rockies?

articles.title: Brewers' Pat Murphy Appears to Rip Yankees in Trending Video From World Series Celebration
articles.summary: Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy has never been shy about offering a take before winning a World Series, so it's no surprise his filter is even less engaged after his team captured their first-ever championship on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy has never been shy about offering a take before winning a World Series, so it's no surprise his filter is even less engaged after his team captured their first-ever championship on Wednesday.

After the Brewers' 4-1 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 5 of the World Series, Murphy appeared to take a dig at the New York Yankees while embracing Jake Bauers.

"Just remember when you were on that horses--t Yankees team," Murphy says to Bauers. "Everyone playing for themselves. Just remember."

After spending the 2022 season in the minors, Bauers returned to the big leagues in April 2023 with the Yankees. He appeared in 84 games for New York that season, then was traded to Milwaukee in November 2023.

The 2022 Yankees weren't a bad team, by any means. They won 99 games and reached the ALCS before losing to the eventual World Series champion Houston Astros.

It's also worth pointing out at that point in Bauers' career, he wasn't considered a starting-caliber player. He hit .202/.279/.413 with the Yankees and had a career slash line of .211/.302/.361 in 412 MLB games from 2018 to '22.

After struggling in his first year with Milwaukee, Bauers revamped his swing going into 2025. The changes have paid off handsomely, culminating in his breakout 2026 with a .266/.389/.484 line in 144 games.

Bauers carried that momentum into the playoffs with a .983 OPS in the NLCS against the Los Angeles Dodgers to win MVP of that series.

A team that could have used Bauers' production this season was the Yankees, particularly in the playoffs when they scored just five runs in a three-game sweep at the hands of the Rays in the ALDS.

New York has the ability to bring Bauers back since he is set to hit free agency this offseason.

articles.title: Way-Too-Early Predictions for the 2027 MLB Playoffs and World Series
articles.summary: Rarely does a team make winning the World Series look as easy as the Milwaukee Brewers just did. They won 103 games during the regular season and then went 11-2 in the postseason. Take a bow, gents.
articles.body:
Rarely does a team make winning the World Series look as easy as the Milwaukee Brewers just did. They won 103 games during the regular season and then went 11-2 in the postseason. Take a bow, gents.

With that done, now we can talk about who's winning it all in 2027.

This exercise is every conceivable kind of "way too soon." The 2026 World Series literally just ended. Have some respect for the Tampa Bay Rays, who aren't even cold yet. Sheesh.

Oh, there's also a lockout looming. Nobody knows when the next competitive games will be, much less what the underlying structure of Major League Baseball will look like. It's been a long time since baseball has had such an uncertain future.

Yet because the baseball gods demand predictions, we are duty-bound to make them. We'll just have to take a lot about the 2027 season for granted and mix boldness with humility. After all, our predictions from last year aged about as well as you'd expect.

We'll go division by division, asking the big questions and projecting final standings as we go.

The Biggest Unknown: How will the New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox and Toronto Blue Jays pivot?

One supposes what we have here are three big unknowns, but let's not split hairs. All three of these clubs had big hopes for 2026 after making the playoffs in 2025, only to fall prey to a Monty Python-style foot squish :

Toronto Blue Jays: Finished in last place

Boston Red Sox: Embarrassed in the Wild Card Series

New York Yankees: Embarrassed in the Division Series

All three have "I'll be back" energy to some degree or another, though the Yankees' is the least inspiring. They'll do stuff this winter, sure, but they're also running it back with Aaron Boone and Brian Cashman for reasons only they know. To boot, Aaron Judge couldn't stay healthy and will soon be 35 years old.

The Blue Jays, meanwhile, have the most to fix this winter. Namely, an offense that finished last in MLB in scoring and a pitching staff that was gutted by injuries. It's not an enviable task in the slightest.

So, dare we say don't sleep on the Red Sox?

They finished third overall in Wins Above Replacement this year, and that was with next to nothing from Garrett Crochet and Roman Anthony. Them being healthy in 2027 bodes well enough, and even more so if Boston leverages its financial and trade capital to bring in a big name or two during the offseason.

Will the Rays continue to operate on a tight budget, even if it means risking trades of key contributors such as Yandy Díaz and Bryan Baker?

What even is Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at this stage of his career?

Are the Orioles prepared to subtract from their surplus of bats to add starting pitching? If so, keep an eye out for Gunnar Henderson rumors.

Franklin Arias could crack Boston's Opening Day lineup in 2027, but it might mean getting Trevor Story out of his way first.

The Biggest Unknown: What can the Detroit Tigers do to reestablish themselves?

Coming into 2026, the AL Central was supposed to be the Tigers' division to lose. They were coming off back-to-back playoff runs, and FanGraphs put their odds of another berth at 60.2 percent.

Instead, they finished in fourth place and traded Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize along the way. They're sure to remain elsewhere this winter, and Gleyber Torres and Jack Flaherty could depart as well.

You'd think that the brass would want to get aggressive to get the Tigers back on track, but that word hasn't been associated with this franchise in a long time. Owner Chris Ilitch is not as willing to spend as his late father, and president of baseball operations Scott Harris comes off as similarly risk-averse.

Make no mistake, though: This team is not going away.

An offense with Kevin McGonigle, Max Clark and Riley Greene? That'll play, and at least Framber Valdez, Troy Melton and Jackson Jobe are still around on the mound. A.J. Hinch really doesn't need many new toys to play with to return this team to contention in 2027.

Will Steven Kwan still be with the Guardians in 2027? They say yes , but it's hard to actually see it.

Are the Royals going to blow it up? Or, are they going to treat back-to-back years of diminishing returns as a problem they can fix?

Can the Twins trade their way (i.e., Royce Lewis, Trevor Larnach) to more wins, or will they have to push their comfort zone in free agency?

Do the White Sox have it in them to make a proper splash for starting pitching upgrades?

Cleveland Guardians (83-79, No. 6 AL seed)

The Biggest Unknown: Can the Seattle Mariners fix everything that broke?

The Mariners darn near went to the World Series in 2025, and we were convinced that they would get there and win it when we did this last year.

Instead, they reduced us to Kurtz at the end of Heart of Darkness . The horror. The horror. Any given 76-86 season can do that, yet this one took on an unusually strong sense of doom that only got worse as time went on.

The Mariners need to turn the page, and hiring a better manager than Dan Wilson (shouldn't be too hard) is just the start. How such a talented pitching staff only had a 4.20 ERA requires a full investigation. The offense and defense deserve to be set ablaze for crimes against baseball, but big fixes via free agency and the trade market will have to do.

To that end, Jerry Dipoto can throw his weight around if he wants to. There's room in the budget for at least one big signing, and the club's trade capital includes multiple spare arms and a whole bunch of talented prospects.

Granted, Dipoto is normally another risk-averse type. But since even he seems to know his seat is hot , there's no time like the present to finally go all-in.

Just how far to the east will Randy Arozarena end up fleeing?

With both their GM and manager roles vacant, we still need to find out who, exactly, will be running the Astros in 2027.

The A's are set to move to Las Vegas in 2028, so is now the time to push the envelope? Or do they wait?

How soon can Stan Kroenke put his stamp on the Angels? After all, the sale of the team isn't quite final yet.

Do the Rangers double down on a roster that's starting to show age? Or do they look to maybe trade Corey Seager and/or Jacob deGrom?

The Biggest Unknown: Are the New York Mets going to get this offseason right?

It must be really frustrating to be a fan of the Atlanta Braves or Philadelphia Phillies. They're the good teams in the NL East, yet all anyone talks about is those less-than-amazin' Mets!

[Accepts stack of cash from Big New York Sports] Sorry, but this is just how it is.

The Mets have ranked first or second in the league for payroll every year since 2022. They're also run by David Stearns, who laid the foundation for what the Brewers are today. He and owner Steve Cohen should be an unstoppable force… and yet, here we are wondering what they'll do after an 88-loss season.

Investing in pitching is a no-brainer, specifically in the sense that the Mets seem like the best landing spot for Tarik Skubal. Maybe that would be enough, given that Nolan McLean is already in place to be a co-ace.

For the offense, there is no better center of gravity than Juan Soto. But just in case, it would be best not to assume Francisco Lindor and Bo Bichette will be better in 2027. Another hitter is a good idea, perhaps especially if said hitter comes from Japan and is named Teruaki Sato.

The Phillies badly need to shake up their aging core, but it won't be easy to trade Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber even if they want to.

Do the Braves need to move on from Ronald Acuña Jr.? Or has that ship sailed along with his peak trade value?

The Marlins could be a contender if they batten down the hatches and build around their stars. But if they trade Otto Lopez and/or Xavier Edwards instead, nobody will be surprised.

The Nationals need a lot of pitching—probably more than they can secure in a single offseason. So, do they trade CJ Abrams while the getting's good?

The Biggest Unknown: Can the Milwaukee Brewers keep from breaking up the band?

Here, you will find no Brewers slander. Not after what they just did. Wire-to-wire excellence and on a budget? Heck yes. Brewers for President, 2028.

Alas, a certain aspect of their reputation precedes them to such an obvious degree that the following conversation started before the final out of the World Series was recorded: Will they keep all their core players this winter?

The Brewers generally don't let their stars reach free agency, and that has meant trading Corbin Burnes, Josh Hader, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta in advance of their dates with the open market. Should they follow the same template this winter, William Contreras and Trevor Megill would be next.

On one hand, the Brewers have earned the benefit of the doubt even if they do pursue trades of those guys this winter. This year was not a one-off. The Brewers have made the playoffs in eight of the last nine seasons. This is a well-oiled project.

On the other hand, is it too much to ask that they make this winter an exception to the rule? Even if there is a lockout looming, winning the World Series is supposed to be good for business. Perhaps that should not mean business as usual in Milwaukee.

The Cubs badly need to upgrade their pitching staff. That should mean pursuing Tarik Skubal. Alas, it probably won't.

Joey Votto thinks the Reds should trade Elly De La Cruz. Do they dare take his advice?

The Pirates got close to making the playoffs for the first time since 2015, but further progress in 2027 will hinge on fixing Paul Skenes.

The Cardinals surprised people this year, but they'll need to decide whether it's worth accelerating their rebuild under Chaim Bloom. If not, expect Masyn Winn and Iván Herrera rumors.

Milwaukee Brewers (98-64, No. 2 NL seed)

The Biggest Unknown: What will the Los Angeles Dodgers' wrath be like?

The Dodgers got their fourth 100-win season of the 2020s this year, but they didn't get their three-peat. And now, they're staring down a nasty labor fight that will largely be about bringing them to heel . Whatever shall they do?

"I welcome it," the Dodgers' president of baseball operations said after his team was swept by the Brewers in the NLCS. "People saying that we're done and we're on the downside of this run—it's just more noise to us."

Actually, nobody is saying that… yet the point is well-taken, if for no other reason than obviously the Dodgers are in for a big winter. It may well be their last chance to go full-Dodgers before the new CBA, and they do need to make the most of it.

The pitching staff needs reinforcements, and the offense needs to get younger and more athletic. Don't be surprised if they retain Tarik Skubal, and they're sure to be involved in the market's top trade targets as well.

As for Shohei Ohtani, they need to have the attitude that this season showed them how not to handle the four-time MVP. If he's going to continue as a two-way star, they simply have to come up with a better plan to keep both acts sustainable.

The Padres have new owners who seem all-in on bringing the World Series to San Diego. How far are they willing to go to make good? Far enough to keep Michael King? Far enough to replace him with Tarik Skubal?

The Diamondbacks need to figure out what to do with Ketel Marte. Keeping him sounds like a bad idea. Selling low on his trade value may not be a better idea.

The Buster Posey-Tony Vitello Giants already feel like a failed experiment, and we'll be darned if there are any obvious ways to fix that.

Whatever the Rockies can do to escape their 100-loss doom loop, trading Hunter Goodman may not be it. And yet, it may be their best hope for a better future.

Los Angeles Dodgers (102-60, No. 1 NL seed)

AL1: Cleveland Guardians (6) over Detroit Tigers (3) AL2: Tampa Bay Rays (5) over New York Yankees (4)

NL1: Atlanta Braves (3) over New York Mets (6) NL2: San Diego Padres (4) over Chicago Cubs (5)

AL1: Seattle Mariners (2) over Cleveland Guardians (6) AL2: Boston Red Sox (1) over Tampa Bay Rays (5)

NL1: Milwaukee Brewers (2) over Atlanta Braves (3) NL2: Los Angeles Dodgers (1) over San Diego Padres (4)

AL: Boston Red Sox (1) over Seattle Mariners (2) NL: Los Angeles Dodgers (1) over Milwaukee Brewers (2)

Boston Red Sox (1) over Los Angeles Dodgers (1)

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: 'Best Catcher in The World,' Brewers' William Contreras Hypes Himself After World Series MVP Win
articles.summary: Modesty isn't necessary when you've just been named the World Series MVP.
articles.body:
Modesty isn't necessary when you've just been named the World Series MVP.

The Milwaukee Brewers secured their first World Series title with a 4-1 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night. Catcher William Contreras got singled out for his performance across the five games and was understandably riding a high.

"I don't want to offend any of the other catchers in the league. The last thing I want to do is offend any of them," he said through an interpreter, per the Associated Press' Ronald Blum . "But sitting up here today, champion of the world, I feel like I'm the best catcher in the league. Again, that's no disrespect to any of them. That's the last thing I want to do. But today I feel like I'm the best catcher in the world."

Contreras batted .381 and had a .435 on-base percentage in the World Series. Blum noted how his contributions behind the plate might have surpassed his offensive production. The three-time All-Star threw out four base stealers and correctly challenged 10 out of 13 pitches.

Some will push back on Contreras' assertion that he's the best catcher in the game.

His 3.0 WAR ranked fifth at the position at FanGraphs , well behind the Arizona Diamondbacks' Gabriel Moreno in first (5.4). There's also the question of how much Cal Raleigh's reputation should take a hit after the Seattle Mariners catcher fell off badly from his 2025 performance.

But Contreras earned the right to brag after playing such an important role in a championship triumph.

articles.title: Brewers to celebrate 2026 World Series title with Friday parade
articles.summary: The Brewers clinched the first World Series in franchise history on Wednesday night against the Rays.
articles.body:
Milwaukee will get its first sports championship-related parade since 2021 on Friday when the Brewers celebrate their 2026 World Series title.

Five years after the Bucks delivered an NBA championship, the Brewers and their fans will have their opportunity to continue to revel in the team's first World Series title (and the city's second after the 1957 Braves) with a Parade of Champions beginning at 11 a.m. ET.

Two days after the Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 to clinch the series in Game 5, the Commissioner's Trophy will be in attendance as the festivities are set to run through downtown Milwaukee and conclude at Henry Maier Festival Park.

During his postgame press conference, Brewers manager Pat Murphy jokingly asked two of his sons, Austin and Jaxon, whether their little league baseball duties might interfere with attending the parade.

Pat, Austin and Jaxon will be joined by team alumni during the festivities. There will also be a special showing of "Ueck," the documentary about legendary Brewers broadcaster Bob Uecker.

There will also be a Championship Rally at American Family Insurance Amphitheater inside the park.

Should some fans be unable to attend, the parade will be streamed on MLB Network, MLB and Brewers.com.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Brewers manager Pat Murphy rips Yankees while being given the baseball from the last out
articles.summary: Pat Murphy doesn't think too highly of the way one other MLB team approaches the game.
articles.body:
The 2026 World Series was a long time coming for Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy. The 67-year-old got his start as a baseball coach in 1982 and didn't get a full-time managerial gig in the majors until 2023.

After such a lengthy climb to reach the pinnacle of the sport, Murphy was — understandably — a bit more willing to let loose following the Brewers' championship-clinching win in Game 5 on Wednesday.

He got that opportunity — and didn't disappoint — upon being presented with the final-out baseball from Game 5. That moment was captured on video, as Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers walked over to Murphy and gave the manager the baseball that secured the last out of the 2026 World Series.

Murphy embraced Bauers for the gesture, and then delivered one more piece of sage advice to his first baseman, one that came at the expense of the New York Yankees.

Content warning: Video contains some NSFW language.

And just in case you didn't catch that, here's what Murphy told Bauers:

"You're going to be a rich f***er. Just remember when you're on that horses*** Yankees team and you're all playing for yourselves, just remember this is the way we used to do it."

Bauers, 31, turned in a breakout season with the Brewers in 2026. The lefty hit .266/.389/.484, with a career-high 26 home runs, during the team's championship season. After signing a one-year, $2.7 million deal with the Brewers last offseason, Bauers is set to be a free agent in a few days. His breakout should earn him a fair amount of looks from bigger-market teams, ones that can outspend the Brewers and give Bauers a ton of money.

One of those teams could be the Yankees. The club could be in the market for a first baseman this offseason, especially one who can take advantage of the team's short porch in left field.

While Murphy's comment was directed at one team, the Yankees were just the example he used to highlight what he sees as a larger narrative in baseball right now. The reason for the Brewers' success in 2026, in Murphy's eyes, is that every player on the team played for the team, not for individual accolades. The manager doesn't think that's a common sentiment around the league.

You can chalk that up to typical manager speak, though at least Murphy's teams seem to live up to that idea. The Brewers have rarely been seen as the most talented team in baseball during his stretch as a manager, but he's consistently produced a win total much higher than the level of talent on the team suggested was possible. Perhaps those extra wins are the result of Murphy's insistence that the Brewers play a selfless version of baseball?

Regardless of what drove the Brewers' success the past few years, Murphy has earned the right to talk some smack following the team's World Series win. It's up to the 29 other MLB teams to figure out how much they want to heed his advice.

articles.title: Michael King Reportedly Opts Out of Final 2 Years, $58M of Padres Contract, Buyout Details Revealed
articles.summary: After re-signing with the San Diego Padres on a three-year deal last offseason, starting pitcher Michael King will be searching for a new home this winter.
articles.body:
After re-signing with the San Diego Padres on a three-year deal last offseason, starting pitcher Michael King will be searching for a new home this winter.

Jon Heyman of the New York Post and MLB Network reported on Thursday that King has declined the final two years and $58 million remaining on his deal with the Padres and will become a free agent after receiving a $5 million buyout.

ESPN's Jeff Passan previously reported that King would be one of the top starters in free agency if he opted out, so he could be in line for a significant payday.

1 Player Every Team Must Re-Sign in Free Agency 💰

The Padres originally acquired King from the New York Yankees prior to the 2024 season as part of the Juan Soto blockbuster trade. After primarily serving as a reliever for the first five years of his career, he transitioned to being a full-time starter upon his arrival to San Diego, and he quickly became one of the team's most reliable pitchers.

After finishing his first year with the Padres with a 13-9 record, a 2.95 ERA and a career-high 201 strikeouts across 31 appearances with 30 starts, King was limited to just 15 starts in 2025 due to various injuries. He bounced back nicely this season, starting all 32 of his appearances and finishing with a 12-10 record, a 3.21 ERA and 159 strikeouts.

With King leading the rotation, the Padres went 91-71 this season and earned a wild-card spot before losing to the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. He made three appearances (two starts) during the postseason, allowing one run on five hits with 15 strikeouts in 14.0 innings.

Losing King to the open market would hurt San Diego's chances of remaining competitive against the elite teams in the NL if he signs elsewhere, but the 31-year-old will likely have a ton of suitors before he cashes in this offseason in a major way.

articles.title: Brewers Should Resist Trade, Push to Keep World Series MVP William Contreras amid Latest MLB Rumors
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers are no doubt still letting loose amid the champagne-soaked celebration of their first ever World Series title.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers are no doubt still letting loose amid the champagne-soaked celebration of their first ever World Series title.

Unfortunately, the business side of the MLB world waits for no one, so at least some of the organization's attention must already shift toward difficult offseason decisions.

And given how tricky some of these decisions will be, that attention has probably been there for a while.

Contreras: I'm 'Best Catcher in The World'

How tricky, you ask? Well, with 2027 free agency likely awaiting World Series MVP William Contreras, their history says they'll seriously consider trading him away now to avoid the risk of watching him walk for nothing later, a route previously taken with Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta.

The Brewers do, at least, "believe they will have more money at their disposal after the World Series run," per The Athletic's Andy McCullough and Will Sammon .

While that should give them "more flexibility in spending on player salaries," it won't change their reality. "A significant deviation from the organization's roster-building model is unlikely," the reporters noted.

Unless labor negotiations change everything, Milwaukee's financial constraints will remain. Before the World Series started, Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold relayed that "making sure this is sustainable" was an edict delivered from owner Mark Attanasio.

The Brewers were 19th overall in payroll this season, per Spotrac. They could substantially up their spending and still not crack the sport's top 10.

They aren't printing money. They can't cover up any roster holes with piles of cash.

They have to work within their margins, which historically has required them to subtract marquee stars ahead of huge paydays and find cheaper, younger, cost-controlled alternatives.

That can work when viable options are at the ready. That just isn't the case with Contreras.

Milwaukee's farm system might be stacked— fifth-best in the bigs according to B/R's post-draft rankings—but it doesn't have a Contreras clone.

His bat is bag. His defense is lights-out. His reliability nears ironman-status. His edge-setting leadership might be most valuable of all.

He is the kind of high-end, follow-my-lead talent who is worth breaking the mold to keep.

Is it risky? In a way, sure. The Brewers could demand top dollar in a trade and expect nothing less. The baseball world is paying premiums for catchers ( remember what Adley Rutschman fetched? ), and Milwaukee would have a premium one to offer.

The prospect of losing Contreras, though, would match that risk and multiply it by 100. Because it's not just taking his bat out of the lineup or removing his presence from behind the plate.

It would be getting rid of the guide who just helped steer this squad farther than it had ever been. The economics of keeping Contreras won't be easy, but they are absolutely worth figuring out. Whatever he is worth in a trade, he's worth far more on the diamond and in the clubhouse.

articles.title: MLB labor FAQ: With a lockout on the horizon, here's what baseball fans need to know
articles.summary: The current CBA expires on Dec. 1. It's highly unlikely that the league and the players' union reach a new deal before then.
articles.body:
The baseball playoffs just delivered fans an exhilarating month of highlights and heartbreaks on a daily basis, but looming over the postseason was the threat of a work stoppage because the collective bargaining agreement (CBA) between Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association is set to expire soon, and the two sides are far apart when it comes to negotiating a new deal.

With a lockout on the horizon, let's break down what's going on with the CBA. Here's everything fans need to know.

The CBA, which is essentially the employment contract negotiated between MLB team owners and the players' union, expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. It was signed on March 10, 2022.

If MLB and the owners institute a lockout, it means that they have instituted a work stoppage and a freeze on communication between the two sides until a new CBA is agreed to. During a lockout, all player activity is halted, and neither trades nor free-agent signings can take place. Also, players are not allowed to have communication with any team personnel, including training and medical staff.

In a memo sent to league employees in early October, MLB outlined how club owners and executives should operate during a lockout and went as far as to say that they should not send holiday cards to players, but they can still attend players' weddings. A lockout is typically lifted when a new collective bargaining agreement is agreed to, voted on and ratified by the union. — Dorsey

What's the difference between a lockout and a strike?

A strike and a lockout are both forms of work stoppages. The difference is which party institutes it. A strike occurs when the players, led by the MLBPA, decide to withhold their services and refuse to play. Strikes don't happen often in baseball, with the most recent coming in 1994 and famously leading to the cancelation of the World Series that season.

A lockout occurs when the league and body of owners do not allow labor, in this case players, to report to work. When the last collective bargaining agreement expired on Dec. 1, 2021, MLB team owners imposed a lockout.

Both strikes and lockouts are forms of negotiating tactics, enacted with the hope of inducing quicker action, gaining leverage and pushing one side's cause and demands. A work stoppage does not guarantee that regular-season games will be missed, but it is a possibility. The start of spring training and spring training games could also be impacted in 2027. — Dorsey

What is the main point of contention between the league and the players' union?

A salary cap, which is a limit on the total any one team can spend on player salaries.

For years, the idea of a salary cap has been such a nonstarter for the players' union that it has rarely sustained as a sticking point in CBA negotiations. Instead, the league and its owners have pursued other avenues to level the playing field — and more broadly improve their financial standing. The most obvious mechanisms for that have been the luxury tax, which has been adjusted dramatically in recent years to add thresholds that punish teams with outlier payrolls by charging overage taxes and negatively impacting draft positioning.

The most recent CBA also featured other wins for club owners: the expansion of the postseason from 10 to 12 teams (the league was pursuing a 14-team postseason field, but the two sides met in the middle), the allowance of advertising on team helmets and uniforms, and the introduction of a Joint Competition Committee made up of six ownership representatives, four players and one umpire, which paved the way for MLB to have the majority needed to institute a huge wave of rule changes (pitch timer, shift restrictions, pickoff limits, among others) without interference from players.

But this time, with the backdrop of the Dodgers' back-to-back championships fueled in part by their exorbitant payroll, the league appears more motivated than ever to push for a salary cap, even with the small-market Milwaukee Brewers winning the 2026 World Series. — Shusterman

Management's desire for a salary cap is the headliner and deservedly so; it would be the most fundamental alteration to the sport in decades. That new system, based on an MLB proposal from the summer , would also include a salary floor.

The league is, in this window of bargaining, firmly on the offensive. While cap-related topics will dominate much of the discourse and debate throughout the winter, there are multiple other changes the league hopes to implement. In its most recent proposal, released Oct. 8, MLB introduced the idea of a 154-game regular season , a seven-game division series, a weekly off day and higher-seeded playoff teams selecting their opponents in the first two rounds.

Other league propositions include but are not limited to:

A reduction in pre-free-agency years from six to five for players 30 or older

A "cornerstone player" system similar to the NBA's Bird Rights

More restrictions on roster modifications

An offseason signing window and offseason transaction freeze

A total overhaul of how amateur players, in both the domestic and international markets, matriculate into pro ball. — Mintz

The MLBPA appears to be seeking more modest changes compared to the enormous transformations offered by the league. Unsurprisingly, most of the union's messaging thus far has been focused on warding off a salary cap. They have made it clear that any system involving a cap is a flat-out nonstarter for the players.

Since bargaining commenced earlier this year, the MLBPA has submitted distinct proposals featuring a smattering of pro-player details, including:

Significant increases to minimum salaries

Stricter guardrails to protect against service-time manipulation

A new "competitive integrity" tax on teams that fail to spend above a certain level

Expansion of active rosters from 26 to 28 players early in the season in an attempt to protect players from injury

A ban on prop bets targeted at individual players in hopes of reducing gambling-related harassment

It's worth noting that most of these specific proposals, from both sides, are just negotiating posturing. Some might be implemented as proposed; most won't be. They make for juicy headlines, yes, but we're still far too early in the process to know how realistic any of these offerings will be. It's all about the cap, anyway. — Mintz

When the previous CBA between MLB and the MLBPA expired on Dec. 1, 2021, the league instituted a lockout, beginning baseball's first work stoppage in more than 25 years. From that point, more than three months of long, tenuous negotiations between the league and the union took place. After being locked out for 99 days, MLB and the MLBPA agreed to a new collective bargaining agreement on March 10, 2022.

That agreement led to a chain reaction of events in early March. First, there was a flurry of transactions, as free agents looked to find new homes and teams were finally allowed to make trades and signings to fill their rosters. Then spring training opened on March 13 with spring training games beginning March 17. Opening Day was pushed back from March 31 to April 7. All 162 games were played, the regular season ended on Oct. 5, and the final game of the World Series was played on Nov. 5. — Dorsey

What dates do fans need to know this winter?

Dec. 1 is going to receive the most airtime, but the team owners locking out the players on that date is a fait accompli. Don't expect a flurry of negotiation between the two sides leading up to the deadline. It's more likely that LeBron James requests a trade to the Cincinnati Reds than that the union and league settle things before Dec. 1.

The next critical guidepost will be the week of Feb. 9. That's when pitchers and catchers typically report to spring training complexes, about 45 days before Opening Day. The passing of that date won't trigger anything tangible in regard to bargaining, but it will serve as a symbolic moment, with players likely to still be home at that juncture.

About a month after that — let's call it the week of March 10 — is probably the most important cutoff on the calendar. That's when the lack of resolution on a new CBA would necessitate a revision of the 2027 regular-season schedule. During the last labor cycle, the agreement on March 10 delayed Opening Day by one week, but MLB still crammed in 162 games by pushing the postseason back as well.

This time around, there might come a point when a 162-game season becomes unviable. Given that players need at least a few weeks of spring training-style ramp-up, that line in the sand is probably around March 15. You can push back the season only so far before the league is playing World Series baseball in a mid-November blizzard. — Mintz

Probably not. In July, MLB announced that the 2027 regular season is scheduled to begin with "Opening Night" on Wednesday, March 24, followed by a full Opening Day slate on Thursday, March 25. But again, using the lockout five years ago as a reference point, these dates could be altered should negotiations drag on.

On March 1, 2022, with negotiations still stuck in the mud, Manfred penned "a letter to baseball fans" in which he stated that "the calendar dictates that we are not going to be able to play the first two series of regular season games and those games are officially canceled." After another week of talks without a resolution, MLB announced that more games were being eliminated from the schedule, stating that "because of the logistical realities of the calendar, another two series are being removed from the schedule, meaning that Opening Day is postponed until April 14th."

That sounded rather definite at the time, but once a deal was reached on March 10 — three weeks before the originally scheduled Opening Day — both sides agreed on a compressed spring training and adjusted regular-season slate that featured additional doubleheaders (and a later finish) and allowed clubs to play all 162 games while delaying the start of the season by only eight days.

Recent history and the current climate make it unlikely that Opening Night on March 24 will take place as scheduled, but it's impossible to say just how delayed the regular season could be — and learning from past experience, declarations that games are officially canceled should not be taken at face value. That said, the limits of flexibility required to squeeze in all 162 games remain unclear. And given the contentious nature of the talks to this point, it's quite possible that there will be increased willingness from both sides to accept a shortened schedule, not just a compressed one. Clarity in this regard is unlikely to come until March.

As of now, Opening Day 2027 is still March 24. But plan something joyful for that day. There probably won't be baseball to watch. — Shusterman

articles.title: Red Sox Make 1st Trade of MLB Offseason, Latest Rumors on Deal with A's After World Series
articles.summary: Less than 24 hours after the World Series wrapped up, marking the end of the 2026 MLB season, the Boston Red Sox and Athletics made the first trade of the offseason.
articles.body:
Less than 24 hours after the World Series wrapped up, marking the end of the 2026 MLB season, the Boston Red Sox and Athletics made the first trade of the offseason.

Per USA Today 's Bob Nightengale , the Red Sox are trading veteran outfielder Nate Eaton to the Athletics.

Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com added Boston will receive a minor leaguer back in the deal.

1 Player Every Team Must Re-Sign in Free Agency 💰

Way-Too-Early 2027 MLB Playoff Predictions 🔮

Eaton even reaching the big leagues was a huge success story for someone who was a 21st-round pick by the Kansas City Royals in the 2018 draft.

It took until 2022 for Eaton to make his MLB debut with the Royals. He showed promise with a .264/.331/.387 slash line in 44 games as a rookie, earning a spot on the 26-man roster to start 2023.

After struggling to start the season, Kansas City demoted Eaton to Triple-A where he played for the rest of 2023 and '24. He opted for free agency at the end of 2024 and signed a minor-league deal with the Red Sox.

Eaton got an extended look in Boston during the 2025 season. He hit .296/.348/.383 in 41 games and made the postseason roster, starting the first two games of the AL Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.

He spent most of 2026 in the minors, though he did once again finish the year with the MLB club and started Game 2 against the Yankees in the wild-card round.

Eaton's ability to play all three outfield spots and third base will give the A's more flexibility with their roster. The 29-year-old will likely slot in as their fourth outfielder next season.

Tyler Soderstrom, Lawrence Butler and Henry Bolte are set to start in the outfield for an A's team looking to rebound after a disappointing 64-98 record this season.

articles.title: Astros' Tatsuya Imai Reportedly Makes Decision on Contract Option for 2027 MLB Season
articles.summary: Former NPB star Tatsuya Imai is reportedly opting in to at least one more season with the Houston Astros.
articles.body:
Former NPB star Tatsuya Imai is reportedly opting in to at least one more season with the Houston Astros.

Imai is not taking the opt-out available on his contract after 2026, the New York Post 's Jon Heyman reported Thursday.

1 Player Every Team Must Re-Sign in Free Agency 💰

Imai is set to receive $18.7 million in salary from the Astros next season, per Spotrac .

The pitcher also holds an opt-out after the 2027 season. Should he decline and accept another $18.7 million for 2028, he could hit free agency ahead of his age-31 campaign in 2029.

Imai signed a three-year, $54 million contract with the two player options on the back end with the Astros after a strong 2025 season with the NPB's Seibu Lions.

He struggled through his first three MLB starts, capping off the run with an appearance during which he recorded just one out while allowing three runs and four walks before he was pulled with the bases loaded. Imai was then placed on IR with right arm fatigue.

The pitcher came back in April and made 12 starts, recording a 5.58 ERA over 50 innings before manager Joe Espada told reporters July 31 he was moved to the bullpen.

Imai went on to make eight relief appearances over the rest of the season, recording a 2.00 ERA in 18 innings in the final two months of the campaign.

He was on the roster for the Astros' Wild Card series against the Chicago White Sox, but the team was swept before he made an appearance.

Imai said in August through an interpreter adjusting to MLB had been more "difficult than I thought," per The Athletic's Chandler Rome .

The interview came after Imai spoke early in the 2026 season about difficulties in adjusting to playing in North America ranging from ball size to mound texture, cooler temperatures and meal times, per MLB.com's Max Ralph and Brian McTaggart .

"For my second year, it won't be my first year, so I'll have to adjust well more and start performing with more consistency," Imai said in August, per Rome.

Imai was one of the NPB's best pitchers in 2025, earning a 10-5 record and recording a 1.92 ERA across 163 2/3 innings.

The Astros have starters including Hunter Brown, Peter Lambert, Cristian Javier and Hayden Wesneski set to return next season. Whether Imai is able to take another step toward replicating his NPB success in North America this summer could impact whether he gets another shot at joining them or returns to the bullpen next season.
